← THE DECLARATIONARTICLE II OF XXVII
GRIEVANCE II ◆ PUBLIC TRUST

He has invited great private fortunes to finance alterations to the people’s house, without full public accounting.

THE RECORD SHOWS

The White House ballroom has attracted hundreds of millions of dollars from donors, including companies with federal business, under a system criticized for opacity.

Documents reported by The Washington Post identified roughly $333 million in private commitments. Reuters reported contributions from major technology companies and federal contractors. The White House defends the privately funded project; watchdogs warn that incomplete donor disclosure makes influence difficult to assess. Donations do not, by themselves, prove a quid pro quo.

A DOCUMENTED SEQUENCE

3 MILESTONES
  1. April 2026A contract governing ballroom fundraising was reported to permit anonymous giving and limit conflict-of-interest checks.
  2. June 2026Lawmakers questioned separate taxpayer spending on White House security in connection with the project.
  3. October 2026Documents examined by The Washington Post identified $333 million in private donor commitments, including major corporations with federal interests.

WHAT THE RECORD DOES NOT ESTABLISH

Reported private commitments, projected total construction costs, and federal security allocations are different figures. The allegation that public funds support the project remains disputed; donor connections do not alone establish corrupt exchange.
